props.title: The People vs. Larry Flynt

sections.content: The People vs. Larry Flynt (1996) stands as one of Hollywood's most compelling examinations of First Amendment rights, with Miloš Forman masterfully directing Woody Harrelson as the controversial Hustler magazine publisher. The film follows the same provocative spirit as other landmark free speech films like Lenny (1974) and Good Morning, Vietnam (1987), but pushes further by forcing viewers to defend the rights of an arguably unsavory figure. Harrelson's nuanced performance transforms Flynt from a simple smut peddler into a complex crusader for constitutional rights.

sections.content: The film shares DNA with other vital legal dramas about individual rights like Erin Brockovich (2000) and Philadelphia (1993), but Forman's direction elevates it beyond standard courtroom fare. The Czech director, who fled Communist censorship, brings personal weight to scenes of Flynt's legal battles. Courtney Love's raw performance as Althea Leasure adds tragic depth, while Edward Norton's controlled turn as Flynt's lawyer Alan Isaacman provides the film's moral compass.

Like All the President's Men (1976) and Spotlight (2015), the film demonstrates how protecting controversial speech ultimately safeguards all speech. The Supreme Court scenes, particularly Flynt's landmark case against Jerry Falwell, rank among cinema's most powerful depictions of constitutional law in action. Forman's camera work during these sequences emphasizes both the grandeur of American justice and its accessibility to even its most notorious citizens. SUBHEAD: The Personal Cost of Public Rights

sections.content: The film excels in showing the personal toll of Flynt's crusade, echoing similar themes in Malcolm X (1992) and Milk (2008). The assassination attempt that leaves Flynt paralyzed, his wife's tragic descent into addiction, and his own struggles with pain medication create a complex portrait of sacrifice for principle. These personal elements elevate the film beyond pure legal drama into a meditation on the price of freedom.
